item.title: On Afro-Asian Radicalism — Thu Sep 3, 4:30 PM — Rubenstein Library Carpenter Conference Room 249
item.description:
The complex strand of Black radical thought found in Japan pulsates with dynamism that can move in different directions. This talk suggests how to relate to this object of knowledge, or Afro-Asian radicalism. I see this task as an exercise in probing a deep well of commitment suffused with political defeats but also yearning to learn, evolve, and advance found within the intervening space between Black radicalism and Japanese intellectual and creative activities in the twentieth century.
In Japanese, an interstice is defined as ma (間). Attunement toward such a point of entanglement is of utmost importance to Afro-Asian radicalism. The details will be culled from Black Radical Thought in Japan (University of Washington Press, 2026), which delineates Japanese intellectuals' commitment to Black struggle cultivated through the study and translation of Black texts, many connected to the midcentury U.S. Left.

item.description:
Join NCWF South Wake Conservationists Chapter for a presentation about chimney swifts! In 1682 a swift was found nesting for the first time in a chimney at a colonist’s cabin in Maine. This event forever changed the relationship between chimney swifts and people. From the journals of early explorers through the efforts of the largest all-volunteer research project to study the migration of a single species of bird, to Jesuit missionaries in a far-off land, it’s a remarkable story. And it’s not over. It’s a story whose next chapter will be written by us. REGISTER HERE

item.title: Southeast Bumble Bee Atlas Survey (Gatesville) — Sun Sep 6, 8:30 AM
item.description:
Volunteers of all ages are invited to buzz on over and join NCWF Wildlife Habitat Stewards of Northeastern NC Chapter for a Southeast Bumble Bee Atlas survey at Merchants Millpond State Park! The Xerces Society created this community science program to empower people across the country to help monitor bumble bee populations and collect important habitat data. Our native pollinators face a series of threats from habitat loss, pesticide use, and climate change to low genetic diversity and the introduction and distribution of disease. To help track population changes that can inform conservation management, scientists need all of the support they can get from dedicated volunteers like you! We’ll have all the survey supplies you need to support pollinator conservation in our corner of North Carolina as we monitor in the chapter’s adopted priority block at Merchants Millpond State Park.
REGISTER HERE

item.title: Invasive Stiltgrass Removal at Merchants Millpond (Gatesville) — Sun Sep 6, 10:00 AM
item.description:
Join NCWF Wildlife Habitat Stewards of Northeastern NC Chapter for a morning of hands-on habitat restoration as we work together to remove invasive Japanese Stiltgrass along the Coleman Trail. This project helps protect the park’s long-term ecological health and prepares the area for a native plant installation later this fall. Japanese Stiltgrass (Microstegium vimineum) is an invasive annual grass introduced to the U.S. in the early 1900s, likely through contaminated packing materials. It spreads quickly along trails, floodplains, and forest understories, forming dense mats that crowd out native understory plants. As it takes over, it reduces habitat quality for insects, amphibians, reptiles, and groundnesting wildlife making active removal an important step in restoring a healthy, thriving ecosystem. REGISTER HERE
Source: NC Wildlife Federation

item.title: Sustainable Labs Interest Session — Wed Sep 16, 9:00 AM
item.description:
Campus labs and research are incredibly important to the University, but they're also very water and energy intensive. In fact, campus labs are the largest consumers of water and energy on campus. Started in 2009 as the Green Labs program, Sustainable Carolina has revamped the program and given it a new name: Sustainable Labs.
The program focuses on key areas (waste, energy and water, freezers, chemicals), and is designed not to shame labs or lab personnel for waste or energy intensive equipment, but rather to identify small steps labs can take to be more sustainable and to recognize all the steps that labs have already taken.
This interest session for Sustainable Labs will be led by Langley Smith, Sustainable Carolina’s program specialist. We invite lab managers, students who work in labs, and faculty to join us and learn how their labs can participate in the program.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.title: Healthy AI Use: Avoiding an Echo Chamber — Thu Sep 17, 9:00 AM — 79 Degrees West
item.description:
An AI affirms your position ~49% more than a person would, and even one agreeable exchange hardens your conviction that you're right. Early research suggests that even when we become aware of this, it doesn't reduce how influential our AI can be. We inherently trust AI (and people) that flatter us, and this module goes deeper into what that leads to, how to audit it happening, and where you can rebuild boundaries or rules for healthy, structured habits.

item.title: Luminary & Freedom Stories — Fri Sep 18, 7:00 PM — Bennett Place State Historic Site
item.description:
During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States.
Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War.
---
Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'"
Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. Some took enormous risk to reach Union lines before the federal government made any promise of abolishing slavery. Others left their homes and plantations to follow Sherman's army as they marched

item.description:
Volunteers of all ages are invited to buzz on over and join NCWF Wildlife Habitat Stewards of Northeastern NC Chapter for a Southeast Bumble Bee Atlas survey at Merchants Millpond State Park! The Xerces Society created this community science program to empower people across the country to help monitor bumble bee populations and collect important habitat data. Our native pollinators face a series of threats from habitat loss, pesticide use, and climate change to low genetic diversity and the introduction and distribution of disease. To help track population changes that can inform conservation management, scientists need all of the support they can get from dedicated volunteers like you! We’ll have all the survey supplies you need to support pollinator conservation in our corner of North Carolina as we monitor in the chapter’s adopted priority block at Merchants Millpond State Park. item.description:
Join NCWF Triad Wild Chapter and log your last summer hike at Hanging Rock State Park (and hopefully spot some early signs of autumn during the last weekend of summer!) This 3-mile hike shows off some of the lesser-hiked parts of one of North Carolina’s oldest state parks. With a 429-foot elevation change, hikers are encouraged to consider the climb and descent. The hike will be worth it; ascending among the boulders, hikers are rewarded with views overlooking Winston-Salem, Greensboro, and even High Point visible on a clear day! As hawk and raptor migration couples with fall bird migrations, bird activity will be near its peak. Birders may get to catch a last glance of summertime birds like the summer tanager, black-and-white warbler, and great-crested flycatcher while hawks and falcons pass overhead! Leaves will begin showing signs of fall colors to come, with the green peaks and valleys of summer still visible before the cold season kicks off. REGISTER HERE

item.title: Aho Branch Planting (Blowing Rock) — Mon Sep 21, 1:00 PM
item.description:
Join NCWF High Country Wild and Blue Ridge Conservancy for a workday along Aho Branch at BRC’s Conservation Campus. The Campus, located between Boone and Blowing Rock, has become a community hub with a rain garden for stormwater runoff, native landscape around the office, half acre pollinator garden trail, 2.2-mile public hiking trail, shrub transition zone for wildlife habitat between the forest and field, and an agricultural plot growing food for the community. During this workday, we will direct our effort toward planting native plants and building deer proof cages to contribute to the larger ongoing stream and wetland restoration project on campus. This project will transform a former cattle grazing pasture into healthy aquatic and terrestrial habitat with riparian and vernal pool plantings along 800 linear feet of Aho Branch. Numerous wildlife species will benefit from this project including yellow-spotted salamanders and brook trout. REGISTER HERE
